Predicting Mentions of Gender Inequality

Phase 1


Human Forecasting

In this phase, we aim to capture your independent human reasoning, without prior knowledge of the empirical patterns identified by our machine-learning analysis.






In this task, the goal is to predict whether a paper discusses gender inequality.



A paper is classified as discussing gender inequality if its title or abstract contains at least one gender inequality keyword.


	Examples of gender inequality keywords: patriarchy, male dominance, gender identity, gender stereotypes, sexism, gender biases, sex discrimination


 



We have collected 13 features for each paper. You may refer to the tables below or to this feature list, for detailed definitions of each feature.



Disciplinary domains

Cl


	
		
			Feature Name
			Data Type
			Description
		
	
	
		
			social_science
			Binary
			Equals 1 if the paper is published in a journal whose scope lies within social sciences (e.g., sociology, political science, psychology, economics, history, philosophy), and 0 otherwise.
		
		
			natural_science
			Binary
			Equals 1 if the paper is published in a journal whose scope lies within natural sciences (e.g., biology, chemistry, physics, environmental science, medicine), and 0 otherwise.
		
		
			engineering_and_technology
			Binary
			Equals 1 if the paper is published in a journal whose scope lies within engineering and technology (e.g., engineering, computer science, applied mathematics), and 0 otherwise. 
		
	





Author demographics

Cli


	
		
			Feature Name
			Data Type
			Description
		
	
	
		
			num_authors
			Integer                         
			Total number of authors of the paper.
		
		
			female
			Continuous in range (0, 1)
			The estimated share of female authors on the author team. For each co-author, we infer the probability of being female based on their first name and then calculate the average probability across all co-authors.
		
		
			asian
			Continuous in range (0, 1)
			The estimated share of Asian authors on the author team. For each author, we infer their most likely country of birth based on their last name. Using the racial composition of that country, we estimate the probability that the author is Asian. The final score is the average of these estimated “Asian probability” values across all co-authors.
		
		
			black
			Continuous in range (0, 1)
			The estimated share of Black authors on the author team. For each author, we infer their most likely country of birth based on their last name. Using the racial composition of that country, we estimate the probability that the author is Black. The final score is the average of these estimated “Black probability” values across all co-authors.
		
		
			hispanic_and_other 
			Continuous in range (0, 1)      
			The estimated share of Hispanic and other-race (i.e., other than Black, White, and Asian) authors on the author team. For each author, we infer their most likely country of birth based on their last name. Using the racial composition of that country, we estimate the probability that the author is Hispanic or another race (i.e., other than Black, White, and Asian). The final score is the average of these estimated probabilities across all co-authors.
		
		
			white
			Continuous in range (0, 1)
			The estimated share of White authors on the author team. For each author, we infer their most likely country of birth based on their last name. Using the racial composition of that country, we estimate the probability that the author is White. The final score is the average of these estimated “White probability” values across all co-authors.
		
	





Diversity measures

Cli


	
		
			Feature Name
			Data Type
			Description
		
	
	
		
			authors_race_diversity_score
			Continuous
			
			The average racial diversity within the co-author team, measured by Shannon entropy.

			

			For each author, we first infer their most likely country of birth based on their last name. Based on the country’s known racial composition, we assign each author a 4-dimensional race-composition probability vector over the four racial categories (Asian, Black, Hispanic_and_other, White).

			

			To compute the diversity score, we first average these probability vectors across all authors to obtain a team-level racial distribution. We then apply Shannon entropy to this averaged distribution.

			
				Higher values indicate a more balanced mix of racial groups within the author team.
				Lower values suggest dominance by a single racial group within the author team.
			

			See here for the detailed calculation.

			
			
			
		
		
			country_race_diversity_score
			Continuous
			
			The average racial diversity of the authors’ countries of birth, measured by Shannon entropy.

			

			For each author, we first infer their most likely country of birth based on their last name. Based on the country’s known racial composition, we assign each author a 4-dimensional race-composition probability vector over the four racial categories (Asian, Black, Hispanic_and_other, White).

			

			To compute the diversity score, we first calculate Shannon entropy for each author’s probability vector. We then average these entropy values across all authors.

			
				Higher values indicate that, on average, the authors come from countries with racially balanced populations.
				Lower values mean that the authors tend to come from countries dominated by a single racial group.
			
			See here for the detailed calculation.
		
	




For example, a paper with authors whose inferred countries of birth are racially homogeneous (e.g., China, Norway, or Japan) will typically have a low country_race_diversity_score. Yet it can still have a high authors_race_diversity_score if the model assigns different race probability profiles to different authors—for instance, one author’s profile places more weight on Asian, another on Black, and another on White.




Time-lagged measures

Cl


	
		
			Feature Name
			Data Type
			Description
		
		
			news_inequality_mentions_3_years
			Continuous
			The average percentage of news articles mentioning inequality across all forms—including gender, racial, economic, and general inequality—over the three years preceding the paper’s publication year. 
		
		
			paper_inequality_mentions_3_years
			Continuous
			The average percentage of academic papers mentioning inequality across all forms—including gender, racial, economic, and general inequality—over the three years preceding the paper’s publication year.

Second, I focus on Black, which I perceive as one of the most prominently discussed forms of racial inequality globally. column30:
My line of reasoning structures around 3 main categories that are represented in the choices that I have made:
- Negative predictive effects for natural and hard sciences (natural_science, engineering_and_technology). I believe that the predictive effect should be negative as natural sciences such as mathematics and physics, tackle topics that are almost completely unrelated to racial concerns, as they are purely interested in abstract and mathematical theories that help advance their own field of study. However, a note of uncertainty in my reasoning lies in the fact that major "natural science" journals such as Nature, Science, PNAS, allow for broad interdisciplinary papers to be included within the journal, which would then concern many topics within the domain of racial concerns. If by natural_science, you only care about journals exclusively tackling mathematics, physics and theoretical fields of study, then my reasoning holds.
- Positive predictive effects for race diversity (authors_race_diversity_score, country_race_diversity_score). This is pretty intuitive and relates to the idea that the more salient a social issue is, the more inclined people are to think about it and study it. Countries that are highly diverse in ethnic population, will have much larger ethnic or racial social issues due to the nature of it's inequality structure (such as France, the UK, USA, Canada, etc), whereas highly homogenous countries often focus more on social issues within a collective racial ethnicity (Japan, China, South Korea). For instance, while both such countries study gender inequalities, I would not be surprised to find much more papers on gender inequality or gender differences in the homogenous countries relative to racial papers, whereas in diverse countries, racial AND gender papers might be closer in proportion. Authors' own personal racial diversity could also play a large role, mainly due to the fact that a larger more diverse co-author environment, is indicative of a diverse environment in either the country of origin, or country of employment. This surely influences the saliency of racial concerns towards an author.
- Positive association to social_science due to the nature of the field itself. This should also be very intuitive as social science related fields are fundamentally involved with the question of social harmony, equality, morality and interindividual differences. Not only are racial concerns fundamentally associated with the fields involved (economics, psychology, sociology, politics, etc), but furthermore, racial concerns have been very salient in these fields through previous mentions of it in research papers and through direct association with it in textbooks. I am strongly led to believe that people would publish or conduct research on racial concerns, and that more so, people interested in racial concerns would also lead themselves to study social sciences.

I would like to note however in the race diversity and social science categories, that there is also the legal issue involving whether authors are allowed to collect data on racial related information in participating individuals. For instance, France treats racial data in a highly sensitive manner, often disallowing researchers to handle it entirely for experimental studies. This might slightly affect my line of reasoning (although due to the majority of research being conducted in the US, I stand by my initial arguments)

The theoretical importance and ranking of these features are grounded in the principles of standpoint epistemology and sociocultural agenda-setting. The "Black" identifier is ranked as the primary predictor based on the assumption that a researcher’s lived experience and social identity—often referred to as positionality—are the strongest drivers of their research agenda; scholars from marginalized groups are theoretically the most likely to dedicate their intellectual labor to investigating the structures of their own marginalization. This is followed by the "News Inequality Score," which reflects the cultural zeitgeist. The reasoning here is that academic inquiry does not happen in a vacuum; a heightened public and media focus on inequality creates a feedback loop of institutional funding and social urgency that nudges researchers toward these topics.

The "Social Science" designation is ranked third, serving as the necessary methodological container; while identity and environment provide the "why," this discipline provides the specific qualitative and quantitative tools required to analyze race as a social construct. The "Author Race Diversity Score" and "Country Race Diversity Score" follow as secondary environmental factors. The assumption is that diverse collaborative teams and heterogeneous national contexts increase the "salience" of race, making it a more frequent subject of academic scrutiny through constant exposure to cross-cultural frictions. I anticipate a positive sign for all five features: as the researcher’s identity aligns with the subject, the media environment emphasizes inequality, and the disciplinary and demographic contexts become more diverse, the statistical probability of the paper focusing on race inequality increases. This reflects a belief that research is a direct byproduct of the scholar's identity filtered through their socio-political and institutional environment.

Test 1: Positional knowledge and the Black authorship effect
My theory predicts that Black scholars are drawn to racial inequality research through positional knowledge and lived experience. To test this, I would run a logistic regression of racial inequality mention (Y) on black, controlling for social_science, female, asian, white, num_authors, and year_of_publication fixed effects. If the positional knowledge mechanism is correct, the coefficient on black should be positive and significant even after controlling for discipline and other demographics. To further probe this, I would split the sample by discipline: the coefficient on black should be positive within both social science and non-social science papers, since lived experience with racial issues should motivate research on racial inequality regardless of disciplinary setting.
Test 2: Natural experiment using the killing of George Floyd (2020)
The murder of George Floyd in May 2020 represents a plausible exogenous shock to the public salience of racial inequality. My theory predicts that heightened societal attention to inequality translates into more academic engagement with racial inequality, and that this effect operates primarily through social scientists. I would create a binary indicator post_floyd equal to 1 for papers published in 2020 and 0 for papers published in 2018-2019 as the control period. I would then estimate a difference-in-differences style regression: Y on post_floyd, social_science, and their interaction post_floyd * social_science, controlling for author demographics. My theory predicts a positive coefficient on the interaction term, meaning that the increase in racial inequality mentions after Floyd's killing was disproportionately concentrated among social science papers. A positive main effect of post_floyd would also support the broader claim that societal events drive academic attention to racial inequality.
Test 3: Country-level racial diversity and exposure to racial dynamics
My revised theory holds that authors from racially diverse countries are more attuned to racial inequality because of exposure to multiracial societies. I would regress Y on country_race_diversity_score, controlling for social_science, all author race shares (black, asian, white, hispanic_and_other), female, num_authors, and year fixed effects. The key test is whether country_race_diversity_score retains a positive and significant coefficient after controlling for the individual race composition of the author team. If it does, this supports the idea that growing up in a racially diverse society has an independent effect on research orientation toward racial inequality, beyond simply being of a particular racial background. If the coefficient becomes insignificant after adding race share controls, it would suggest that country_race_diversity_score is merely a proxy for author race composition rather than capturing a distinct exposure mechanism.

My theory argues that Asian scholars engage with racial inequality research because of racialized minority experiences in Western academic institutions. To test this mechanism more directly, I would want a binary variable indicating whether each author is affiliated with a US-based institution. If the mechanism is correct, the positive effect of asian on racial inequality mentions should be concentrated among Asian scholars working in the US, where racial discourse is most salient. I would interact asian with a US_institution indicator in a logistic regression predicting Y. A positive and significant interaction would support the claim that it is the experience of being a racial minority in a Western context, rather than something inherent about Asian identity, that drives engagement with racial inequality research. If the interaction is insignificant or the asian effect is equally strong outside the US, this would challenge my proposed mechanism.

Additional variable 2: Author's prior publication history on inequality topics
My theory relies heavily on positional knowledge as a mechanism linking author demographics to racial inequality research. But an alternative explanation is simply path dependence in research agendas. A variable capturing whether each author has previously published papers mentioning inequality would help disentangle these stories. I would include a prior_inequality_publications count or binary indicator and interact it with black and female. If positional knowledge is the primary driver, then black and female should retain significant positive effects even after controlling for prior publication history. If instead the coefficients on black and female shrink substantially after adding this control, it would suggest that the demographic effects operate primarily through established research trajectories rather than identity-driven motivation per se.

Additional variable 3: Funding source or grant type

A variable indicating whether a paper was funded by a grant specifically related to diversity, equity, or social justice would help test whether the patterns I observe are driven by supply-side researcher motivation or demand-side institutional incentives. I would include this as a control in the main regression and also interact it with social_science and post_floyd. If funding is doing much of the work, adding it as a control should attenuate the effects of social_science and the time-lagged inequality mentions. If the existing predictors remain strong after controlling for funding, this would support my theory that researcher identity and disciplinary orientation are the primary drivers rather than external funding incentives.

The ML results align with my expectations on three of the five features. Social_science and female appearing as the top two predictors with positive signs is consistent with my theory that disciplinary framing and positional knowledge are the primary drivers of gender inequality research. Paper_inequality_mentions_3_years also appeared in my original selection with the same positive sign, confirming that broader academic trends in inequality discourse do matter for gender inequality research.

The appearance of natural_science with a negative sign is not surprising in substance but I did not select it as a top five feature because I viewed it as essentially the flip side of social_science. A negative effect of natural science is logically consistent with a positive effect of social science since both capture the same underlying idea that inequality research is concentrated in social science disciplines. I would not have expected natural_science to carry independent predictive power beyond what social_science already captures, but it is possible that the Random Forest finds additional discriminatory value in explicitly flagging natural science papers as unlikely to discuss gender inequality, even among papers that are not classified as social science.

The positive sign on asian is the most unexpected result, just as it was for racial inequality. I initially selected white as a predictor based on the reasoning that Western feminist traditions are institutionally rooted in predominantly white academic contexts. The ML evidence suggests that Asian authorship is more predictive than white authorship. One possibility is that Asian scholars working in Western institutions engage with gender inequality research as part of a broader engagement with social justice topics, similar to the pattern observed for racial inequality. Another possibility is that gender inequality is a salient research topic in many Asian countries due to well-documented gender disparities in education, labor force participation, and political representation, which may motivate Asian scholars to study these issues regardless of institutional context.

The absence of white from the top five challenges my initial reasoning about Western feminist traditions. It may be that white authorship is too common in the dataset to be a strong discriminator, or that the institutional traditions I attributed to whiteness are better captured by the social_science variable itself.
column83:
Gender inequality is a social phenomenon, so the discipline of a paper is likely important and hence social_science would be a predictor. Papers published in journals covering sociology, political science, economics and psychology are probably very likely to engage in inequality research, including gender inequality specifically. The ML evidence also shows that natural_science carries an independent negative effect, suggesting that being in a natural science discipline actively reduces the likelihood of discussing gender inequality beyond simply not being in social science. This may reflect that natural science journals have norms and scoping conventions that discourage engagement with social topics even when individual researchers might be interested.
Since scholar identities shape their research agenda, female authors are likely to explore inequality, and as a consequence, gender inequality within their research. This mirrors the positional knowledge argument: women scholars have direct lived experience with gender-based disparities in academia and beyond, making them more likely to pursue research on gender bias, gender discrimination, and related topics.
I am updating my theory to replace white with asian as a predictor. My initial reasoning about Western feminist traditions being rooted in predominantly white academic contexts was not supported by the ML evidence. Instead, the positive association with Asian authorship suggests that gender inequality is a salient research topic for Asian scholars, potentially because gender disparities in education, labor markets, and political representation are well-documented issues in many Asian countries. Asian scholars may be motivated to study gender inequality both because of conditions in their countries of origin and because of experiences navigating gendered dynamics in Western academic institutions. It is also possible that white authorship is simply too prevalent in the dataset to serve as a useful discriminator, while Asian authorship captures a more specific signal.
The time-lagged academic inequality mentions remain a meaningful predictor, confirming that broader scholarly trends in inequality discourse shape whether papers engage with gender inequality. Events like the #MeToo movement or debates around the gender pay gap can motivate authors willing to write relevant research to focus on gender inequality. However, I note that news_inequality_mentions_3_years did not appear in the top five for main effects, suggesting that media attention may operate more indirectly for gender inequality research compared to academic attention.

The interaction results for gender inequality are identical in structure and sign to those for racial inequality, which is a striking finding. This parallel suggests that the mechanisms linking disciplinary context, societal attention, and author demographics to inequality research operate similarly across both racial and gender domains.

The first two interactions are consistent with my theoretical reasoning. Social_science interacted with paper_inequality_mentions_3_years (+) and with news_inequality_mentions_3_years (+) both confirm that broader societal and academic attention to inequality matters most within social science. Social scientists are the scholars best equipped to respond to rising discourse around inequality, whether in news media or academic publications. When inequality becomes more salient publicly or in the literature, it is social scientists who channel that energy into gender inequality research. Engineers and natural scientists are unlikely to pivot their research agendas in response to media coverage of the gender pay gap or the #MeToo movement. This also explains why news_inequality_mentions_3_years did not appear as a strong main effect but emerges in the interaction: its effect is conditional on disciplinary context.

The negative interaction between female and social_science is again the most surprising result, and again contradicts my initial prediction of a positive interaction. As with racial inequality, I initially expected that female scholars in social science would be especially likely to study gender inequality. The negative sign suggests that female authorship adds less predictive value within social science than outside it. The ceiling effect explanation applies here as well: social science papers already have a high baseline probability of discussing gender inequality, so being female contributes less additional information in that context. But there may also be a more interesting story for gender inequality specifically. Outside social science, writing about gender inequality is a more unusual choice that likely requires strong personal motivation, and being female may be a particularly strong signal of that motivation. A female engineer who writes about gender inequality is probably doing so very deliberately, whereas within social science, gender inequality is a mainstream topic that both male and female scholars regularly engage with. This would explain why the marginal effect of female authorship is actually larger outside social science.

The interaction between social_science and paper_inequality_mentions_3_years (+) is the most important because social scientists are uniquely positioned to translate rising academic discourse around inequality into gender inequality research. When more academic papers are discussing inequality broadly, social scientists have the training, publication outlets, and professional incentives to respond by producing gender inequality research. Scholars in natural science or engineering are unlikely to shift their research focus in response to academic trends in inequality discourse, so the time-lagged academic mentions only have a meaningful effect within the social science context.

The interaction between social_science and news_inequality_mentions_3_years (+) operates through a similar channel. When media coverage of inequality increases, perhaps driven by events like the #MeToo movement or public debates around the gender pay gap, social scientists are the scholars most likely to respond by producing relevant research. The news creates public demand for academic engagement with gender inequality, but only scholars in disciplines that study social phenomena can meaningfully supply that engagement. This also clarifies why news mentions did not emerge as a strong standalone predictor: their predictive power is conditional on the disciplinary setting.

The negative interaction between female and social_science is the most important revision to my initial theory. I originally predicted this interaction would be positive, reasoning that female social scientists would combine disciplinary tools with lived experience to produce more gender inequality research. The ML evidence tells a different story. Within social science, gender inequality is a mainstream research topic that scholars of all genders engage with regularly, so being female adds relatively little additional predictive power. Outside social science, however, writing about gender inequality is a more deliberate and unusual choice. A female engineer or natural scientist who publishes on gender inequality is likely doing so out of strong personal motivation rooted in lived experience, making female authorship a much stronger signal in those contexts. The marginal contribution of identity is greatest where the baseline probability of engaging with the topic is lowest.

Test 1: Positional knowledge and the female authorship effect

My theory predicts that female scholars are drawn to gender inequality research through positional knowledge and lived experience. To test this, I would run a logistic regression of gender inequality mention (Y) on female, controlling for social_science, natural_science, asian, black, white, num_authors, and year_of_publication fixed effects. If the positional knowledge mechanism is correct, the coefficient on female should be positive and significant even after controlling for discipline and other demographics. To further probe this, I would split the sample by discipline: the coefficient on female should be positive within social science, natural science, and engineering papers alike, since lived experience with gender disparities should motivate research on gender inequality regardless of disciplinary setting. However, based on the interaction evidence, I would expect the coefficient to be larger outside social science than within it.

Test 2: Natural experiment using the #MeToo movement (October 2017)

The #MeToo movement represents a plausible exogenous shock to the public salience of gender inequality. My theory predicts that heightened societal attention translates into more academic engagement with gender inequality, and that this effect operates primarily through social scientists. I would create a binary indicator post_metoo equal to 1 for papers published in 2018-2020 and 0 for papers published in 2015-2017 as the control period. I would then estimate a difference-in-differences style regression: Y on post_metoo, social_science, and their interaction post_metoo * social_science, controlling for author demographics. My theory predicts a positive coefficient on the interaction term, meaning that the increase in gender inequality mentions after #MeToo was disproportionately concentrated among social science papers. A positive main effect of post_metoo would also support the broader claim that societal events drive academic attention to gender inequality.

Test 3: The independent negative effect of natural science

My revised theory holds that natural science disciplines actively discourage engagement with gender inequality topics through disciplinary norms and journal scoping conventions, beyond simply not being social science. To test this, I would restrict the sample to papers that are not in social science (i.e., only natural science and engineering papers) and regress Y on natural_science, controlling for all author demographics, num_authors, and year fixed effects. If natural science carries an independent negative effect relative to engineering, the coefficient should be negative and significant. This would support the claim that natural science disciplines have particularly strong norms against engaging with social topics, whereas engineering may be slightly more permissive given its engagement with topics like diversity in STEM. If the coefficient is insignificant, it would suggest that natural_science is simply a mirror of social_science rather than carrying its own disciplinary suppression effect.

Test 4: Asian authorship and gender inequality salience

My revised theory proposes that Asian scholars engage with gender inequality research because of the salience of gender disparities in their countries of origin. To test this, I would regress Y on asian, controlling for social_science, natural_science, female, other race shares, num_authors, and year fixed effects. The coefficient on asian should be positive and significant. Additionally, I would interact asian with country_race_diversity_score. If the mechanism operates through country-of-origin conditions rather than minority experiences in Western institutions, I would expect the interaction to be insignificant or negative, since country_race_diversity_score captures something different from the specific gender dynamics in Asian countries. If instead the interaction is positive, it would suggest that the Asian effect is part of a broader pattern where authors from diverse national contexts are more attuned to inequality of all kinds.
column88:
Additional variable 1: Gender composition of the author's academic department or field

My theory argues that female scholars are drawn to gender inequality research through positional knowledge. But an alternative explanation is that women cluster in subfields or departments where gender inequality is already a common research topic, and the effect is driven by intellectual environment rather than personal identity. A variable capturing the share of female faculty in the author's department or subfield would help disentangle these mechanisms. I would include this departmental gender composition variable as a control alongside female in the main regression. If positional knowledge is the primary driver, the coefficient on female should remain positive and significant even after controlling for the gender composition of the local academic environment. If instead the female effect shrinks substantially, it would suggest that the environment rather than individual identity is doing most of the work.

Additional variable 2: Author institutional location (country of institutional affiliation)

My theory proposes that Asian scholars study gender inequality because of the salience of gender disparities in their countries of origin. A variable capturing the country of the author's institutional affiliation would allow me to distinguish between Asian scholars working in Asian institutions and those working in Western institutions. I would interact asian with a binary indicator for whether the author is affiliated with an institution in an Asian country. If the country-of-origin mechanism is correct, Asian scholars at Asian institutions should be at least as likely to study gender inequality as those at Western institutions. If instead the positive effect of asian is concentrated among scholars at Western institutions, it would suggest that the mechanism operates more through minority experiences in Western academia than through conditions in countries of origin.

Additional variable 3: Journal-level history of publishing gender inequality research

My theory suggests that disciplinary norms in natural science actively suppress engagement with gender inequality topics. A variable measuring the share of prior publications in each journal that discuss gender inequality would allow me to separate discipline-level effects from journal-level editorial gatekeeping. I would include this journal-level history variable alongside natural_science in the regression. If the negative natural_science effect is driven by journal norms rather than researcher preferences, controlling for journal history should attenuate the natural_science coefficient substantially. If the coefficient persists, it would suggest that the suppression operates at the level of researcher self-selection and training rather than editorial filtering.

Additional variable 4: Timing of the author's career (years since first publication)

My theory relies on positional knowledge as a stable feature of scholar identity, but it is possible that career stage moderates this effect. Junior female scholars may be more likely to study gender inequality if they enter academia during periods of heightened attention to gender disparities, while senior scholars may have already established research agendas on other topics. A variable capturing years since first publication would allow me to interact career stage with female and with post_metoo. If career stage matters, I would expect the interaction between female and junior status to be positive, suggesting that early-career women are especially responsive to gender inequality as a research topic. I would also expect junior scholars to show a larger response to the #MeToo shock, since they have more flexibility to adjust their research agendas compared to established scholars with fixed programs of work.

This was a well-designed exercise that made the value of human-ML iteration tangible. The most useful moments were when the ML evidence contradicted my priors, like the negative female-social_science interaction and the appearance of Asian authorship. Those surprises forced me to think more carefully about mechanisms I had taken for granted.

One concern is that the demographic features are all estimated from names rather than self-reported, which introduces measurement error that could bias both the ML results and any downstream empirical tests. It would be worth acknowledging this limitation explicitly when interpreting the findings.

I also think the framework could benefit from a step where participants propose features that are missing from the dataset before seeing ML results, not just after. Some of my best thinking about mechanisms came from considering what variables were absent, and that exercise might generate richer initial theories.

The weights for the specific marginalized groups (female, black, asian) should emerge as robustly positive and statistically significant. My interpretations are based on trying to infer the coefficients of factors in a probability of discussing racial inequality on exogenous factors. Natural science is a strong negative predictor, as racial inequality is generally considered a social science topic, and not considered under natural science purview. Hence a paper being in natural science is a strong negative cause of it discussing race. 

Between different racial groups, I think members of the black community are most likely to discuss racial inequalities as the highest recipients of racial discrimination and hate-crimes. While the Asian community also receives racial judgements, my experience suggests that Asian communities are more geared towards the mathematical and engineering sciences, and they tend to be more docile towards calling out hate. Hispanic authors are between the black and Asian communities, and it is likely that a Hispanic author may avoid writing about racial discrimination to avoid feeding into stereotypes that originate from their race. Members of the white community in academia are generally vocal about racial biases, and are dwarfed generally by their black peers. My conjecture would be, in terms of race, the magnitude of coefficients would be black > white > hispanic > Asian. In fact Asian coefficient could be negative, but I cannot conjecture that without additional empirical evidence.

If a country is relatively diverse, like the US, UK, countries in the EU, etc., then the historically privileged community in academia is likely to be vocal about these issues. Whereas if an author coming from a less diverse country, predominated by one race (historically marginalized or not, say African countries, India, China, Korea, Poland, etc.) is likely to have fewer exposure to the perils of racial inequality, and hence less likely to write about it. (I also think that based on the empirical patterns, historical immigration rates in the author's countries may also be included into this model).

While racial inequality is generally discussed in the social sciences, a paper being in the social sciences does not automatically increase the likelihood of it discussing racial inequality. The direction of association is key here: the likelihood of a paper being in social science is high given that it discusses race, but not the other way round. Thus bidirectional measures of association like correlation coefficient would still be weak, but not insignificant. 

I do not think sex, number of authors, computer science papers and historical trends in academic racial discussions have a significant effect on whether a paper discusses race. The historical trends in academic racial discussions is marginally associated, but not conditionally accounting for articles in the news media. The news media articles, on the other hand, is likely to have significant impact in discussing race (for example the George Floyd incident).

Note: Although my answer is long, it is purely my reasoning, not genAI to help. I write long to help your papers have the best insights possible. I also do experiments, so I suspect not all participants of this experiment will do so (although I wish more did so in my experiments!)

Using my reasoning, my first step was to separate "positively associated" and "negatively associated" features. I believe that "negatively associated" features will have strong predictive power in this specific task. For each, I provide an explanation of why.

First, I believe that those features are positively associated with "gender inequality":
- social_science: The majority of scholarly discussions on gender will be in social science journals. But I believe this will be a "weak" feature, as many papers in social science are not necessarily about gender.
- female: A great proportion of papers on gender are from female-only teams. But this doesn't mean that females primarily write papers on gender. In fact, they don't. Thus, I believe this will also be a "weak" feature.
- white: From my experience, it appears that it is mostly white authors who discuss gender inequality. This issue seems particularly important for them. But most papers written by white authors do not focus on "gender" per se, so it will be a very "weak" feature.
- paper_inequality_mentions_3_years: I believe this will be a "strong" feature with great predictive power, as scholars often draw on prior, recent works to advance their contributions. Hence, this feature is in my top 5.
- news_inequality_mentions_3_years: I believe this can also be useful, but scholars often draw from academic papers, not news. I also feel that news is a late-comer, in that academic papers often discuss topics that news covers many years later (especially for long-term social topics such as race, gender, etc).

Second, I believe that those features are negatively associated with "gender inequality":
- natural_science: I myself studied physics before, and those social topics are not appropriate for such journals. Thus, this will be a very "strong" feature with immense predictive power. This is also in my top 5.
- engineering_and_technology: same reason as above, also in my top 5.
- num_authors: natural science and engineering papers often have a very long list of authors (e.g., all master students who helped are added in the author list). So, the longer the list of authors, the higher the probability that it is not a social_science paper. So this will have a great predictive power, but lower than natural_science and engineering_and_technology, so also in my top 5.
- asian: This might sound weird, but as an asian myself and with good knowledge of the asian community, I have the feeling that gender is not a topic that is seen as central (in particular, many asian females I know think this focus on gender is ridiculous). If you look at CWTS Leiden Ranking, you will find that the majority of natural science top publications now are coming from East Asia (especially China). So asians seem to focus strongly on maths, physics, engineering, etc., and much less on discussions related to gender or race. Furthermore, asians who are in social science also focus less on such topics. Thus, this feature is also in my top 5, as I think it can have great predictive power.

Finally, I believe some features are very "weak", so weak that it is unclear to me if they are positively or negatively associated: black, hispanic_and_other, authors_race_diversity_score, country_race_diversity_score

1. About second-order effects: this dataset is already noisy enough that it is hard to quantify the first-order contributions, and considering second-order effects may introduce additional noise and make the results less plausible or convincing. For example, I predicted most of the order-2 effects correctly (social_science × 3_year measures), BUT WE ARE NOT ABLE TO TELL IF THEY ARE TRULY ORDER-2 EFFECTS, OR ONLY A RESULT OF THE MODEL + REGULARIZATION CHOSEN.

For instance, consider a very simple model: y = a x1 + b x2 + c x1 x2, with x ~ N(1,1), and ground truth a = b = 1. If we do linear regression, we would expect to recover a = b = 1 and c = 0. However, if very strong regularization is applied, we may see c > 0 as well. That is, the model may be learning association rather than a true second-order effect; if variables are positively related, interaction terms may be included as “order-2 results” simply due to artifacts of model choice. Therefore, I suggest we better not emphasize second-order results, or at least be very cautious, because we are not sure whether they reflect genuine second-order effects or only positive association learned through an artifact of the chosen model/regularization. For example, if you add L1 regularization, many effects would shrink to 0, including many second-order terms, which may better represent the ground truth.

2. Black researchers are generally much more underrepresented than Asian researchers, but in both results, Asian ranked higher than Black. In theory, I would expect Black authors to care more about racial inequality than Asian authors. This also points to a data imbalance issue: Black authors are likely fewer than Asian authors in the dataset, so the learning algorithm may downweight the importance of Black, even if the “true” relationship is stronger.

Overall, I believe many of these rankings/results are very sensitive to model choice. It would be better to use multiple models (or multiple regularization settings) to report results; otherwise, from a statistician’s perspective, some results may not seem plausible enough.

column30:
My theory is that first and foremost, articles on inequality are published in social science journals. That's just a base rate -- the topic of social science journals are social topics, and diversity / racial inequality is more a a social topic than anything else. The mechanism here isn't anything psychological but statistical so I am not including a mediator.

Second, inequality being part of the "zeitgeist" (via news articles) will increase its salience and permissibility/popularity (i.e., it is "OK" to write about) in the minds of all researchers -- much like "AI" is all over the news these days. Trends in publications follow trends in what is important in society (e.g., intros and discussion sections usually refer to these, researchers get ideas from everyday life, etc.).

Third, I believe that one's own racial identity may motivate one to research in equality, partly due to a salience argument (as above - if you experience it in your everyday life, you will have more inspiration to research it and tackle it) and partly due to motivation (you likely want to help reduce it for future generations, your kids, your family, your friends, etc.). I have a lay intuition that personal motivation may appear higher for people who identify as Black and Asian, because a larger percentage of published research comes from the US, UK, and China. Since I could only list five factors though, I chose to focus on Black as it seems that is a more dominant racial identity studied in the literature (at least based on my narrow reading/memory of it). I also didn't include Hispanic/Other merely from a statistical prevalence and time standpoint. While that ethnicity surely has faced terrible discrimination recently under the Trump administration with deportations, any motivational or salience mechanism won't appear in the published literature until maybe late 2026 or 2027, which is later than this survey. Further, that population is smaller so it may not have enough power to get picked up on in models.

Fourth, I included Female partly due to my own "sampling". I have no idea if this is true in the population, but it seems that people studying diversity of any kind in my network tend to be female. Sometimes they study gender diversity but often they also study racial diversity. I think the mechanism is actually quite similar to race though: Women may feel more discriminated against (Salience) and want to change that (Motivation) including for social categories not their own (Prosocial).

Finally, I ranked publication prevalence lower than news prevalence because my hunch is the former lags behind the latter -- i.e., researchers' interests are inspired by the news more than the news is inspired by researchers' interests. That said, once a theme becomes popular in publications, it does tend to create a trend (e.g., how we talk about in every job market cycle there are "hot" topics - diversity was "hot" a few years ago, AI is hot now). So it does have influence - just lagged and less so than the news, I think. Here I think the mediator is salience, permissibility / popularity, and motivation (ie if past articles were published on this future articles like mine will be too).

In terms of interaction effects, I believe that news and publication trends will heighten the mechanisms with one's own race (or gender). I.e., in a causal diagram, and arrow would flow from each (news, publication) to the arrow between race (black) or gender (female) to the Y variable.

My theory will be quite similar to my theory for racial inequality.

First, these types of topics are social science topics so will be more likely to be published in a social science journal. Main effect with no mechanism really, besides base rates.

Second, I think as with race one's own gender plays a role here. I ranked this higher than zeitgeist because of my lay belief that talking about gender inequality is a more 'open' or common discussion than racial inequality. So identifying as a woman yourself, and having that lived experience, persists beyond news trends (more than it does from identifying as black yourself). Also, a base rate argument: especially in social science it is more likely to be a woman than to be black. So if lived experience influences you to research inequality (Salience, Motivation) then it will motivate a larger proportion of individuals, and more people on the paper are likely to be women. Relatedly, if you're a senior female researcher researching gender inequality, you probably try to raise up other female researchers and would have them on the paper. (No doubt this happens for race as well, but there is a far smaller pool to draw on, so I didn't include it as a main effect for racial inequality). I'll call this mechanism "Talent Availability".

Third, I rated white as higher. So white women may be more likely to research gender inequality than Black or Asian women, for instance. The mechanism therefore is something like crowding out, or "absence" of other motivation. I'll call this "Non-Competing Motivation".

Fourth, as with my other theory on racial inequality, I believe that what we research and write on is impacted by news trends, or the "zeitgeist" in the world. It makes topics more top of mind (Salience) and OK or even attractive to write about (Permissibility / Popularity).

Fifth, again as with my theory on racial inequality, I believe that what is popular to research becomes a trend that we can jump on - via salience, permissibility / popularity, and motivation. Motivation being that if it already got published, it will be more likely to get published again -- there is reviewer/editor appetite for it. But again I think it is less important that the news as an influence.

In terms of interactions, I believe past news articles and past publications will increase the relationship between Female and Salience, Female and Motivation.

For starters, I assumed that if an author is a woman or Black, that probably increases the chances their work engages with racial inequality. Not because of any hard rule, but just because people's backgrounds and experiences tend to shape what they find interesting or important. If you've lived some of those realities yourself, or you're just more tuned in to questions of justice and fairness, it makes sense you might gravitate toward those topics. That's not just an academic guess, it's pretty intuitive.

I also thought that researchers working in more racially diverse countries would be more likely to write about racial inequality. The logic there is pretty straightforward: if you're surrounded by those conversations in everyday life, they're more likely to show up in your work.

On the flip side, I gave negative signs to how much inequality shows up in the news or in other academic papers from the previous few years. Why? Because a lot of that talk tends to be about inequality more broadly, income, gender, region, not race specifically. column91:
There are some modes of reasoning that can be hard to do as a human -- here I am thinking especially of considering the space of linear individual and interactive effects and how these will affect the outcome of interest. I struggled with this especially because I don't often do linear models in empirical settings, so my intuition for these interaction terms is not strong. My prior says that there is enough verbal analysis of this in the literature that LLMs would do a good job of understanding these relationships well. They would also (likely) create better formed priors as they have access to some general world model which I suspect is stronger than most researchers which focus on just a few topics of interest.

I think humans might offer some valuable forms of divergent thinking which could be refined by LLMs, and I think humans might be able to reason about the sequence of results from some hypothetical experiment better than LLMs. But, I think they would benefit from generations coming from LLMs which could connect to past results and methods. While this seems like it would be a fairly general improvement, I suspect human revision after LLM generation could be especially useful. However, I think that LLMs placed earlier in the generation process can ground thinking into a more reasonable space of ideas. An interesting set of theories to study could be:

1. Theories proposed by human experts after reviewing the machine-learning results.
2. Theories proposed by GenAI modes after reviewing the machine-learning results.
3. Theories proposed by human experts after reviewing the (1) machine-learning results and (2) the revised theories of GenAI models that have reviewed the machine-learning results.

In the social sciences, researchers almost always collect participants’ demographic information: age, gender, race, education, and socioeconomic status. This reflects the notion that demographics matter for understanding the human condition. In the social sciences we study: stratification, hierarchy, schooling, policing, discrimination, inequality, labor markets, and related topics, variables that are both theoretically relevant and relatively easy to collect and analyze are more likely to appear in published papers.

I also think that women tend to research, and be involved in, research on social issues because, compared to other fields, it is often seen as less prestigious or high status, and it can create a less aggressive culture that feels more inclusive and welcoming.

Overall, I think there are more white researchers, so we see their over-representation in any field. But as race-related research becomes more central, I also think we will see more whites in that area as well.

Moreover, I believe that news and papers can have a lasting impact on discourse, on people’s memory, and on what feels urgent or important in the current zeitgeist, and therefore will affect the amount and direction of subsequent research.

A number of thoughts. First, I think the way in which the prompts are done matters tremendously, for both humans and AI. For instance, in these scenarios, humans were nudged away from offering a "third variable" explanation for a positive correlation, but if the LLM may be more motivated to be accurate and thus deviate from that nudge. Also, LLMs have no fatigue, so they may generate more complete explanations and richer theoretical models than their human counterparts. They also will have access to much more literature and lines of reasoning than humans, allowing them to draw on more theories (which may help them choose the best one). On the other hand, I could see a sycophantic AI doing worse after seeing the human experts if it feels the need to conform to the human reasoning.

Finally, perhaps the humans would do best. But I think that would depend on the expert pool (i.e., how expert are they, really?)--if they aren't the most expert in the whole world, they'd be worse than the LLM, but perhaps the truly best humans are still better than the LLMs. Taking a step back, LLMs have outperformed humans on many, many kinds of tasks--I suspect that the theories and reasoning needed to generate good hypotheses here could be performed well by an LLM based on the relevant ideas being in the literature. But also, I think it's possible that the LLM performance would depend on the specific model used (e.g. "thinking" vs "non thinking" models, whether it's engaging in "deep research").

1. past behavior is predictor of future behavior - i.e., autoregressive effect: 
news inequality in past 3 years ==> (+)==> inequality study in the next year.
2. field-specific foci, with gender being a social science domain and construct, with less centrality to the works of STEM fields. Ergo:
social science (vs. non-social science) ==> (+) ==>study of gender inequality
STEM (vs. non-STEM)==> (-) ==>study of gender inequality
3. social identity theory and various other aspects of self-identification would predict that women would be more likely to pursue topics that disproportionally affect them than men. and will be more motivated to focus on these features in the discussion as a possible study limitation, ergo:
female==> (+)==> gender inequality
4. Finally, scientists may be drawn to subjects that appear discussed in the popular media (and vice versa, as popular media/news is most likely reporting on PRIOR social science findings to support any stories on gender inequality). Ergo, a weaker effect here:
news of gender inequality==>(+)==> study of gender inequality. One could extend it to state that past work on gender inequality => news of gender inequality => present discussion of gender inequality.

There are two major concerns for this survey setup:
1. Its too long, and though carefully designed, it results in drop in effort. Asking people to draw diagrams on Qualtrics is also VERY HARD (impossible) and takes on time. Who are the scientists who would volunteer their time to perform such tasks for free (2 hours!) just to be a coauthor (one of 20+ on a paper)? The way it is stacked, Gen AI will ABSOLUTELY show higher performance. This may be the genuine result. But in my case it is simply because I lost much interest after 45 min. And in general, its a VERY BAD practice from the survey design perspective to keep ANY survey, esp for scientists over 30 min. guys, you know this! There will be concerns from the reviewers, too, as you have zero true incentives here to do better. for instance, you could have advertised that scientists could test their intuitions and theories and their knowledge etc... Something to keep people motivated.
2. "marginal effects" can be misunderstood, as the meaning of the term in English can refer to the size of the effect. I don't think this is how you meant it, but this is something to keep in mind. Generally, I found the interactions part very suspect and post-hoc and confusing - I suggest you cut it from analyses entirely. For several variables, there are also curvilinear trends.
3. You never explained what exactly you did for ML analyses. Can I trust your results? What did you use and how? Did you cross-validate them? Out of sample tests?

I’d expect these five to positively predict whether a paper discusses racial inequality. 
In terms of strength, I’d expect social science to be the strongest predictor because racial inequality is fundamentally a social phenomenon and is almost exclusively studied within disciplines like sociology, political science, and economics. 
I’d expect paper inequality mentions to be next as it reflects momentum within an academic field: when inequality discussions in the literature are already elevated, individual scholars are more likely to engage with it, both because it spurs their ideas but also because journals and reviewers become more receptive to such work.
I’d expect news inequality mentions to be next as it captures the role of public discourse in shaping peoples research agendas: greater coverage of racial injustice as we saw in high-profile events like police killings in the US motivates researchers to respond and thus increases the probability that papers published in subsequent years address such topics. 
Next, Id expect black author share to predict but conditional on the aforementioned factors. There are well-documented own-group research effects whereby scholars from minority race groups (especially in the USA) are more likely to study topics directly relevant to their own community experiences. 
Lastly, I’d predict authors' race diversity score to positively predict but also conditional on the first three. It is likely to operate through a related mechanism whereby racially diverse teams may be more likely to coalesce around shared interest in race-related questions. Another reason could be that this measure also reflects more diverse collaborative networks which better position scholar to attract funding and publish work on these topics.

The results partially confirm but also diverge from my predictions. Social science ranking first is fully consistent with my theory and provides validation of the disciplinary domain hypothesis. Black author share appearing with a positive sign also aligns with my expectations, albeit ranked lower than I anticipated.
The most surprising divergences are the absence of both paper and news inequality mentions, and the prominence of author demographic features I did not anticipate. 
Female author share ranking second is unexpected; I associated own-group research effects primarily with Black authors for racial inequality research, but the ML suggests otherwise. Perhaps this reflects broader solidarity dynamics across marginalised groups. 
Country race diversity score and Asian author share also outperforming the temporal features was surprising. The country diversity score may be capturing something about internationally diverse teams being more attuned to racial inequality globally. 
The positive Asian coefficient is counterintuitive given that Asian scholars are not typically the primary focus of racial inequality research in Western contexts — though it may reflect researchers from racially diverse countries bringing comparative perspectives on race.
The absence of temporal features suggests field momentum and media salience may operate more weakly than I anticipated. Its also possible that their effects are absorbed by the demographic features.

The evidence – assuming well validated and robust – could lead me to partially revise my theory. Social science remains the strongest predictor for the same reason as before — racial inequality as a research topic is almost exclusively within social science, making this the strongest structural filter. 
Female author share ranking second was unexpected but theoretically interpretable — female scholars may show solidarity across marginalised groups, making them more likely to engage with racial inequality research beyond their own-group interests. Its also possible that they may be more likely to work on topics that span gender and race. 
Country race diversity score ranking third suggests that researchers inferred to come from racially diverse countries bring cross-cultural perspectives that motivate them to racial inequality as a research topic. 
Asian author share ranking fourth is the most surprising finding — one plausible explanation is that Asian scholars working in Western academic institutions, where they constitute a visible minority, may be more attuned to racial dynamics and motivated to study them. 
Black author share ranking fifth remains consistent with my original own-group research effects hypothesis. I retain my original view that the temporal features — paper and news inequality mentions — are theoretically meaningful predictors, but acknowledge that their year-level rather than paper-level variation may have weakened their performance relative to other features that vary paper-by-paper.

The top two interactions — social science × paper inequality mentions and social science × news inequality mentions — confirm that the temporal features I originally theorised do matter, but operate through interaction with disciplinary domain rather than as standalone main effects. That’s actually coherent: social science researchers may be most responsive to field momentum and public salience, so it makes sense these effects are amplified within social science specifically.

Racial inequality is a subject of study primarily in the social sciences (economics, sociology, social psychology), with less relevance to the natural sciences. I would expect engineering and technology to be less predictive than the natural or social sciences as papers in this area are broadly unlikely to address racial inequality, except to the extent that they might address racial inequality in access to technology and other similar topics.

I would expect author demographics to be predictive to the extent that research topics might be chosen based on their personal relevance to the author. This is most likely to be the case for authors who are directly affected by racial inequality, namely black authors. (Being white is likely to be less predictive as whites likely dominate the author population, and therefore numerically may also constitute a large proportion of authors working on racial inequality, as well as any other topics). Finally, I believe being female may have predictive power for two reasons: first, because women are more represented in the population of scholars in the social sciences (and in particular in sociology and social psychology); and second, because questions of social inequality are among the topics that may be perceived as more "feminine" (because other-focused, communal, etc) and, through the effect of social expectations, likely to attract female scholars.
